The Gulf of Carpentaria is a large, shallow sea in northern Australia, held between Arnhem Land to the west and Cape York Peninsula to the east. Dutch ships charted it in the early 1600s; the first recorded European landing in Australia, in 1606, was on its Cape York shore. It is named after Pieter de Carpentier, a governor-general of the Dutch East Indies.

Many Aboriginal peoples live along its coasts and rivers: the Yanyuwa around the Sir Edward Pellew Islands, the Garrwa and Gangalidda in the south, the Marra in the west, and the Kokobera and Kok Narr on the Cape York side. They fished, hunted dugong and turtle, and moved between coast and inland with the wet and dry seasons. Makassan trepang fishers from Sulawesi visited its western shores for generations.

Cattle stations spread around it from the 1860s. Its coast of mangroves and salt flats still has few towns.
